stop_condition: the round-3 findings adjudicated, plus a targeted review of the daemon retirement and the in-process run_with_timeout rewrite that the fix round introduced beyond the findings' scope

findings.evidence: Verified by reading: the supervision loop's condition is `kill -0 "$child_pid"` and the normal path waits only for that PID; the process group is terminated only while the wrapper is still alive at the deadline. So a command that backgrounds its real work — the canonical shape being `sleep 1800 &` — lets the `bash -c` wrapper exit 0 immediately, and run_with_timeout returns 0 while the reparented child keeps running indefinitely in the isolated process group. The isolation also places that child outside the caller's original group, and the hook installs no signal-cleanup trap. Process outcome inferred from standard bash asynchronous-command semantics; the code path itself was read.
findings.description: The timeout is defeated and the function reports success while the work it was supervising is still running — in the one function every verification this plugin performs flows through (tests, lint, type-check). It can also strand tree-mutating verification work that continues after the gate has already reported. This is the batch's own defect family sitting in its most load-bearing place, introduced by the daemon-retirement rewrite rather than by any earlier round.

findings.evidence: The stated wall-clock cap is implemented as a count of completed one-second polls. Each iteration's scheduling delay and heartbeat work falls outside the counted second, so 1200 completed ticks can take materially longer than 1200 seconds under load. More seriously, a stalled `lease_heartbeat`/`touch` blocks the supervisor loop itself, so the deadline cannot fire at all. Verified by reading; drift not measured.
findings.description: A timeout that is a tick count rather than a clock reading silently lengthens exactly when the machine is busy — which is when a timeout matters. And making the supervisor perform the heartbeat couples the deadline's liveness to the filesystem operation it is supervising.

findings.evidence: The heartbeat counter resets to zero for every spec, so a tier lasting many minutes but composed entirely of sub-30-second specs never refreshes its lease. After 90 seconds a second host sharing the hostname can misread the first runner's foreign pid as locally dead and reclaim a still-live lease. The replacement controls are real and discriminating, but their single 35-second spec exercises the long-spec case and specifically misses this cumulative-short-spec case.
findings.description: R3-F3 is PARTIALLY FIXED. A single long command does heartbeat throughout — the case the fix was designed for — but the ordinary tier shape (many short specs) does not, which reopens the very collision the active heartbeat was introduced to protect against.

findings.evidence: The lock permanently fails open if its holder dies before :1073: there is no owner record and no stale-lock recovery, so every later wipe waits roughly one second and then performs the read-modify-write unlocked. Two overlapping wipes can then publish the same generation, letting a Stop captured between them miss the later cycle transition. Verified by reading.
findings.description: R3-F2 is PARTIALLY FIXED. Bumping before deleting plus the post-write rollback genuinely narrow the race, but the increment is still not atomic, and this is broader than the code comment's 'extreme contention' disclosure: one interrupted holder leaves the degraded state permanent rather than transient.

findings.evidence: Documentation still describes the removed six-hour heartbeat daemons and their fd-redirect controls as the shipped mechanism; the spec still says 'heartbeat daemon' in two places; and the hook still attributes dispatch to GNU `timeout` in two comments. Static search confirms the implementation is now in-process and the redirect controls were retired.
findings.description: A mechanism-documentation regression created by the retirement: the shipped text describes machinery that no longer exists, so the next reader cannot tell which description is authoritative.
